title: SYSK Selects: Research tips from SYSK
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on research tips and spotting bad science. Josh introduces it as a pick for listeners (noting Chuck's teeth-transition voice). The episode opens with a listener mail from Bianca about research misrepresentation, unpublished negative results, and preregistration, then moves through a "ten signs that study is bogus" list: unrepeatable/unreproducible findings (Center for Open Science replication project), plausible but unprovable observational studies and the 5 percent chance of false correlations, sensational media reporting and initial findings, unsound samples and WEIRD (Western, educated, industrialized, rich, democratic) study participants, very small sample sizes and statistical power, pressure on trainees and throwing out data points, predatory publishing and fake journals, follow the money with climate-skeptic funding examples, fake peer review, and the 'it's a cool story' problem. The episode closes with administrative details thanking listeners for gifts and social media sign-offs.

segments.title: Selects intro by Josh
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick, the research tips episode, and notes Chuck sounds different due to his dental transition at the time.

segments.title: Listener mail from Bianca on research misrepresentation
segments.summary: Bianca's listener mail describes a class discussion on unpublished negative results, preregistration laws, and drug studies skewed by publication bias. It leads into the hosts' ten-signs list from their website.

segments.title: Sign: unrepeatable results and sensational headlines
segments.summary: The hosts advise checking whether a study got follow-up coverage, name trusted science reporters, and discuss the Center for Open Science project that found more than half of 100 psychology studies could not be reproduced, including a study on men judging women's signals of attraction.

segments.title: Sign: plausible but not provable
segments.summary: Observational studies can produce false correlations by chance, as with the type A personality and heart attack study. Researchers who search many variables can cherry-pick results, and media often turn 'maybe' findings into certainties, as with the Mayan city story.

segments.title: Sign: unsound samples and WEIRD participants
segments.summary: Studies with narrow samples, such as only college students or only heterosexual people, are weak. The hosts discuss the WEIRD acronym and a 2010 survey finding that college students make up most study participants relative to their share of the world population.

segments.title: Sign: small samples, power, and reporting pressure
segments.summary: Very small samples give little statistical power, as with a ten-smoker example. Ulrich Dirnagl's push for institutional reform is discussed, along with a survey of trainees feeling pressure to support mentors' work and the problem of dropping data from animal studies.

segments.title: Sign: predatory publishing
segments.summary: Predatory journals charge authors fees after accepting papers without real review. Jeffrey Beall's list of predatory publishers is mentioned, along with fake journals such as Scientific Journals International and a self-awarded prize. The hosts connect the problem to open-access debates and Aaron Swartz.

segments.title: Sign: follow the money and conflicts of interest
segments.summary: Following funding sources can reveal bias. The hosts discuss Willie Soon, a Harvard Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics researcher who denies human-caused climate change and received funding from energy companies, and the Heartland Institute's past work with Philip Morris on secondhand smoke.

segments.title: Sign: fake peer review and sensational framing
segments.summary: Dr. Moon faked peer reviewers by inventing reviewer identities and returning reviews very quickly. Publishers have had retractions due to fraudulent reviews. The hosts close the list by discussing how the 'cool story' framing and initial findings can dominate science news.

segments.title: Wrap-up on science reporting
segments.summary: The hosts summarize that media favor good headlines over scientific rigor and say they are not scientists and make mistakes. They point listeners to HowStuffWorks search for more on research fraud.

segments.title: Administrative details: listener gifts
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners for coffee, handmade bowls, pasta, cards, books, dog treats, and other gifts, and give social media and contact information.
